CN.source: Convention between the United States and the People's Republic of China for the Avoidance of Double Taxation (1984), Article 20 (Students and Trainees): a student who is or was a resident of China and is present in the United States solely for the purpose of education or training is exempt from U.S. tax on '(a) payments received from abroad for the purpose of his maintenance, education, study, research or training; (b) grants or awards from a government, scientific, educational or other tax-exempt organization; and (c) income from personal services performed in that Contracting State in an amount not in excess of 5,000 United States dollars ... for any taxable year.' Clause (b) has no dollar cap; clause (c) caps the employment-income exemption at $5,000. The article gives no standard deduction. (Text read from the treaty PDF published at irs.gov/pub/irs-trty/china.pdf.)

IN.source: Convention between the United States and the Republic of India for the Avoidance of Double Taxation (1989), Article 21 (Payments Received by Students and Apprentices): paragraph 1 exempts payments arising OUTSIDE the United States for maintenance, education or training (not U.S.-source income, so not modeled here); paragraph 2 provides that '[i]n respect of grants, scholarships and remuneration from employment not covered by paragraph 1, a student or business apprentice ... shall ... be entitled ... to the same exemptions, reliefs or reductions in respect of taxes available to residents of the state which he is visiting.' The Instructions for Form 1040-NR (2025), Line 12, apply paragraph 2 as the standard deduction: 'Standard deduction for certain residents of India. Students or business apprentices may be able to take the standard deduction on Form 1040-NR, line 12 ... if they are eligible for benefits under Article 21(2) of the United States-India Income Tax Treaty. They will enter, on Form 1040-NR, line 12, the standard deduction amount found for their filing status on Form 1040 or 1040-SR.' The treaty has no dollar-capped exemption for U.S.-source employment income and no exemption for U.S.-source scholarship grants (paragraph 2 gives the reliefs available to residents, i.e. the IRC 117 qualified-scholarship exclusion, which a payer applies before reporting an amount on Form 1042-S). (Text read from the treaty PDF published at irs.gov/pub/irs-trty/india.pdf.)

source: Student-article provisions of the U.S. income tax treaties with China and India, read from the treaty texts published by the IRS (IRS.gov, United States Income Tax Treaties A to Z). Only the provisions the Form 1040-NR engine models are recorded; a country absent from this file gets no treaty modeling (the engine proceeds without treaty benefits and warns).
